title: In your own words
hookLine: Rebbe Nachman taught talking to God alone in your own language every day

cards: Late at night, outside a small town in Ukraine, in Rebbe Nachman's time. The houses are dark. Out past the last fence, in the fields, a young man is standing alone and talking.
Out loud. Not reading, not chanting. Talking, the way you'd talk to a friend who's been away: about his day, his temper, the money he owes, the thing he can't stop worrying about.
If you walked past you'd think he'd lost his mind. He's following the instructions of his teacher.

teach.b: The teacher was Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, a Hasidic master.
He gave this practice a name: hitbodedut, from a root meaning to be alone.
In his teachings, collected by his student Reb Noson, he says it's a great thing to set aside time every day, ideally an hour, to speak to God alone, in a field or a quiet room.
And he insists on one detail: in the language you actually speak. For his followers, that was Yiddish, not the Hebrew of the prayer book.
The fixed prayers matter, he says, but it's hard for most people to pour out their hearts in a language they don't really think in. In your own words, you can say everything.
Your regrets, your excuses, your hopes, the small embarrassing things. You can argue. You can ask for help with the day's business.
He also says something tender for the days it doesn't work.
If all you can manage is a single phrase, like Master of the world, say that, over and over. Even that is a great thing. The fixed liturgy and this kind of talking aren't rivals.
The Amidah itself, as we saw weeks ago, has a place to add your own request. Rebbe Nachman just made the private conversation a daily appointment. Breslov Hasidim still keep it.
Some go out to forests at night. Some, it's said, walk a city block with a phone to their ear, so nobody stares.

how: Breslov Hasidim and many others practice hitbodedut: a daily stretch of time, often at night or outdoors, spent speaking aloud to God in their own language, alongside the fixed prayers.

o: a fixed prayer said alone without a minyan
silent meditation on a single Hebrew letter
speaking to God alone, out loud, in your own words

p: the student who wrote it down

s: Rebbe Nachman taught that private talk should replace the fixed prayers
the fixed prayers stay; the private conversation is added each day.
he said even one repeated phrase counts
if all you can say is "Master of the world," say it again and again.
his followers spoke to God in the prayer book's Hebrew
he wanted them to use the language they spoke: for them, Yiddish.

games.q: you go out to the field for your daily hour of talking to God, and nothing comes. no words at all. what did Rebbe Nachman say to do?
o: say one phrase, over and over, until more comes.
games.why: even a single phrase like "Master of the world," repeated, is a great thing, he taught.

practice: Find a spot where no one will hear you, a parked car works, and talk for two minutes in your everyday language: if you pray, to God, as you'd talk to a close friend; if not, to the day, or to the quiet.
If you run out of words, repeat one phrase until something else comes.

wordCard.voice: Hitbodedut. Being alone: Rebbe Nachman's daily practice of speaking with God out loud, in the language you think in.

orig.note: Hebrew: being alone, secluding oneself; Rebbe Nachman's name for private prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: master of the world. Even one phrase is enough. Six hundred thirty-three days now.
